11 β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase and Liquorice
Liquorice contains an enzyme that inhibits 11 β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, resulting in sodium and water retention, hyperten-
sion, hypokalemia, and suppression of the renin–aldosterone system.
Irritant Mechanisms
Certain foods have a direct irritant effect on the mucous membranes of the mouth or gut, such as the irritant effect of coffee or curry.
In certain individuals, food intolerance only occurs in the presence of a coexisting medical disorder. For example, the ingestion of
spicy food, coffee, or orange juice provoke esophageal pain in some patients with reﬂux esophagitis. This effect is unconnected to
the temperature or acidity of the food, or to any effect on the lower esophageal sphincter. The treatment in susceptible individuals is
to avoid the trigger food item.
Speciﬁc Drug–Food Combinations
One example of drug-induced food intolerance is potentiation of the pressor effects of tyramine-containing foods (e.g., cheese, yeast
extracts, and fermented soya bean products) by monoamine oxidase inhibitor drugs. Another is the effect of taking alcohol in
patients with alcohol dependence during treatment with disulﬁram (Antabuse). The reaction, which can occur within 10 min of
alcohol and may last for several hours, consists of ﬂushing and nausea.
